extracted.intended_audience: instructors and TAs who give feedback and grade mathematics presentations (undergraduate/graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for giving feedback and assessing student mathematical presentations (timing, style, content, pedagogy), aimed at instructors who must comment on or grade oral talks across math courses. Includes practical advice on feedback specificity, modes of feedback, and sample rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing notes
rubrics_metrics.description: An outline of the talk including the amount of time spent on each portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenting on timing helps students see pacing and allocation of time; useful to give notes immediately after the talk so students can adjust future timing. Useful both for rehearsals and final talks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation style
rubrics_metrics.description: Style of speech, use of visual aids (blackboard/ slides/ images), pacing, audience engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity and audibility of speech, appropriate use of blackboard vs slides, slide design/readability, tempo and pauses, gestures, eye contact, and strategies used to engage the audience. Note positive aspects as well as problems to correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical content
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctness of mathematics and connections of material to other parts of the course or other parts of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out specific errors when appropriate (especially in rehearsals); for final talks, favor general comments and highlight important conceptual links that would deepen understanding or pique interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching strategy (motivation and exposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of motivation, examples, conceptual explanations, repetition, and other teaching techniques to make material accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the presenter provides motivation for results, chooses appropriate examples, balances conceptual intuition with formal development, and uses repetition or signposting to aid understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity / Level of detail in feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the level of detail of comments depending on whether the presentation will be given again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For rehearsals, note every math mistake so the student can fix them. For one‑time final presentations, avoid exhaustive lists of errors that may demoralize; instead give broader, forward‑looking suggestions for future presentations. See the linked 'Dimensions of Commenting' handout for more guidance on choosing wording and level of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form / Mode of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of feedback delivery: immediate written notes, recorded review with one-on-one debrief, whole-class discussion, email or later meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate notes are most time‑efficient; recording and reviewing with the student is highly helpful but time‑intensive; class discussion requires a respectful atmosphere; email allows reflection but may lack clarifying Q&A. Choose based on available time and learning goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine and prioritize grading criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and prioritize grading criteria before grading to prevent unintentional, subconscious bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deciding what matters in advance helps graders be consistent and reduces bias (cites Uhlmann and Cohen, 2005). Use written rubrics or checklists so all graders apply the same priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commenting/grading forms or rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a commenting form or grading form to remind instructors to consider all important aspects of a presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms help prevent focusing only on the most obvious issues, prompt recognition of positives, and produce consistent comments. The page recommends customizing forms so they reflect your priorities rather than using a generic form unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic & Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: (Ball State University rubric category) The structure and logical flow of the presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the talk is focused and structured, whether information is ordered so content flows logically, and whether the presenter guides the audience through the content with clear signposting and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content
rubrics_metrics.description: (Ball State University rubric category) The mathematical substance of the presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess appropriateness and depth of material, correctness, relevance to the assigned topic, and whether connections to broader mathematics are made. Consider balance between conceptual explanation and formal detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: (Ball State University rubric category) The presenter's communicative performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes voice, pace, eye contact, audience engagement, use of visuals, and overall professionalism. Delivery can be separately scored from content and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of performance (basic / good / excellent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive tiers for talk quality (basic expectations, characteristics of a good talk, characteristics of an excellent talk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tiered descriptors to differentiate varying levels of achievement (e.g., what separates a good talk from an excellent one). The page cites 'Characteristics of an effective undergraduate research talk' as an example that outlines expectations at multiple performance levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of the audience's background and use of strategies to engage them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor explanations to the audience, avoid unnecessary jargon, check for comprehension, and use examples or visuals appropriate to the listeners. Engagement may be measured by questions solicited, interactivity, or clarity of exposition for the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance conceptual vs. formal
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate balancing of conceptual explanations with formal mathematics and rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the presenter gives enough intuition for understanding without sacrificing necessary precision; consider the audience and purpose when choosing the balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision, rigor, and proof structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate level of precision and logical structure in proofs or arguments presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For talks that include proofs, evaluate clarity of proof structure, correctness, choice of proof techniques, and whether informal/heuristic arguments are clearly labeled as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness and appropriateness of visual aids (slides, blackboard work, images, diagrams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge readability, relevance, and integration of visuals with spoken exposition. Note common problems (overcrowded slides, unreadable equations, misuse of animations) and highlight good visual design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation: customize rubrics to course goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your own rubric so the form reflects the instructor's priorities rather than using an off‑the‑shelf form unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select categories and weightings that match whether talks are practice/rehearsal, formative assignments, or summative assessments. Sample rubrics on the page (including for proofs, math fairs, and grade‑level talks) may be adapted.
